task_title: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
title: Two calls agreed on the wrong payout: let code compute it
stem: Harbour Mutual's claims agent calculates payouts from garage quotes and pays any amount within its US$5,000 authority. To catch errors, a second Claude call recalculates each payout, and the agent pays only when both agree. An audit finds a payout that both calls agreed on, but that silently left out an unpriced quote line, which kept it under the limit. Which change best addresses this failure mode?

options.A: Move the calculation step to Claude Opus 5.5, whose stronger reasoning makes arithmetic and omission errors much less likely than on a smaller model.
options.B: Add worked examples to the prompt, including a quote with an unpriced line, that show the model how to flag a gap before it calculates.
options.C: Have Claude extract each line with null for missing amounts, then compute the payout in code and hold any claim that has an unpriced line.
options.D: Add a third independent calculation call and pay only when all three agree, routing any disagreement between the calls to an adjuster.

why: The failure mode is a fluent figure produced from input that can't support it, confirmed by a check that shares the same blind spot. The reliable fix splits the work: Claude does what it is good at (reading and copying lines, with null where nothing is printed), and deterministic code grounds each line in the quote, refuses to compute while a line is unpriced, applies the policy terms and checks the authority limit.

wrong.A: A larger model makes errors rarer, not impossible, and it still has to guess an amount the quote doesn't print.
wrong.B: Examples improve the odds but leave the payout resting on the model's arithmetic and its judgement.
wrong.D: More calls of the same model share the same blind spot, so they can agree on the same wrong figure.

fix: Extract the lines with Claude (null where unpriced), then hold, compute and route on the payout in code.
see: Both Phase 1 calls agree on about $4,810.58 and it is paid; Phase 2 holds for line 14, computes $5,340.64 and escalates.
explain: Line 14 of the quote says 'per materials sheet to follow', so no correct payout can be computed from the quote alone. In Phase 1 Claude still returns a figure, about $4,810.58 with line 14 silently left out, and a second call agrees with it. The figure is under the $5,000 authority, so the pipeline pays it without an adjuster. In Phase 2 Claude extracts all 21 lines with line 14 as null; code checks the other 20 amounts against the quote, holds the claim, fetches the materials sheet ($486.30), computes $5,340.64 from the policy terms and escalates it to an adjuster.
exam_tip: Self-consistency (ask twice, compare) and bigger models are tempting answers to an accuracy problem. When the failure is a known mode, such as arithmetic, missing input or a hard business rule, the professional answer is to move that part into deterministic code and let the model do the reading.
headline: The model reads the quote. Code does the sums.

concepts.b: An LLM produces a plausible answer to the question asked, even when the input can't support one. A required number in a schema gets filled, with or without the facts.
Two calls of the same model share the same blind spots. Agreement shows stability, not truth; an independent check uses a different source, such as the document or code.

concepts.t: Arithmetic is a known weak spot
concepts.b: Long sums in one pass are error-prone, more so with thinking off. Bigger models and examples make errors rarer, not impossible. Hard arithmetic belongs in code.
Check each extracted amount against the source text, and require null where the source prints nothing. A value that isn't in the document is a guess.
When a required input is missing, stop and fetch it; don't compute around the gap. Missing data is a reason to route the case, not to estimate.
